title: Humans in the Loop
author: Rebecca Crootof · Margot E. Kaminski · W. Nicholson Price II

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source maps competing views rather than adopting a determinate position. Its discussion of complementary human–AI systems aligns with the cluster’s supervised-copilot framing, but it also reports proposals for institutional oversight and outright machine substitution, without resolving among them or addressing the cluster’s legal-workflow evidence in sufficient depth.
qs: 1, 6, 44– 54 (2019) [hereinafter Pasquale, A Rule of Persons, Not Machines] (suggesting a complementary approach for automation may better realize rule-of-law values than a substitutive approach);

REV., July 26, 2018, https://hbr.org/2018/07/want-less-biased-decisions-use-algorithms [https://perma.cc/6U9Z-VR6J] (arguing for replacing humans with machines); Frank Pasquale, A Rule of Persons, Not Machines: The Limits of Legal Automation, 87 GEO.

st.t: EU governance: Simplification tests enforceable safeguards
st.an: The source accepts the EU’s risk-based governance framework and credits its operational oversight and preventive-design safeguards, while materially developing the cluster’s argument that enforceability requires competent, authoritative overseers and institutional legitimacy rather than nominal human approval. It identifies concrete gaps in binding training requirements, self-certification and reliance on a single person to resolve contested values.
qs: How could deferring to a single person in the loop’s take on contested concepts such as “fairness” and “discrimination” make that process legitimate, when additional voices might define “fairness” or “discrimination” differently, with meaningfully different results?

st.t: Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control
st.an: The source directly accepts the synthesis’s central distinction between nominal human accountability and effective control, then materially develops it into a regulatory framework: define the human’s intended role and ensure usable interfaces, intervention authority, training, resilient handoffs and appropriate allocation of responsibility.
qs: Further, a MABA-MABA response distracts policymakers from more effective— albeit more complicated and difficult—forms of regulation.32         To regulate human-in-the-loop systems well, one must first identify what the human is intended to do.

engineering suggests a need to focus on human cognitive strengths— such as pattern recognition and responsiveness to change––in designing effective informational interfaces between human and machine.330         Machines must also be built to respond to useful human interaction.331 What good is an informational interface if a human has no way to intervene?

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core view that human–AI performance is context-dependent and that nominal human oversight is insufficient. It materially extends the proposition by specifying that human roles, authority and capabilities must be designed explicitly and that governance should target the whole sociotechnical system rather than merely assigning verification to an individual reviewer.
qs: Without understanding the desired role, designing systems for success, creating metrics to track that success, and evaluating success become substantially more difficult.279 Conversely, identifying the intended role(s) fosters systems and organizational design that ensure the human in the loop has the needed authorities and capabilities.

governance to make room for changes over time.397       The question of how to regulate human-in-the-loop systems will remain a constant for the foreseeable future, but the right answers will vary dramatically depending on the roles humans are meant to play and the context of the particular systems.

kp.k: Human oversight requires governing the whole hybrid system
kp.d: The authors offer a cross-domain regulatory framework rather than a prediction about legal employment or an unconditional endorsement of automation. They argue that inserting an individual into algorithmic decisionmaking does not itself ensure effective oversight: policymakers must specify human roles, consider context, and regulate the interacting technical and organizational system.
qs: We advocate neither for nor against delegating a decision to an algorithm or human; instead, we argue that if policymakers are going to attempt to regulate hybrid systems, they need to do a better job.
Namely, rather than carelessly placing a human in the loop, policymakers should regulate the human-in-the-loop system.

kp.k: Formal human involvement need not be effective
kp.d: The article deliberately includes ineffective reviewers within its definition of a human in the loop, exposing the difference between nominal participation and meaningful influence. Examples include physicians using diagnostic tools, lawyers changing e-discovery searches, and humans deciding whether to implement algorithmic recommendations. The authors caution that focusing on the individual decision obscures designers, employers, institutions, and other humans shaping outcomes.
qs: For the purposes of analyzing existing law, we define a “human in the loop” as an individual who is involved in a single, particular decision made in conjunction with an algorithm.
Note that nothing in our definition requires that the human in the loop must be effective.
Humans select training data and inputs. Humans ask the question the system answers.

kp.k: Existing law already shapes automation and human participation
kp.d: The authors identify explicit requirements, inherited professional restrictions, regulatory incentives, liability rules, and legal silence as influences on retaining or removing humans. Examples include prescription rules requiring authorized professionals and traffic conventions assuming drivers. Their survey treats enacted rules, proposals, guidance, and soft law separately; as of publication, they report knowing of no explicit bans on including a human in the loop, although a scholar had proposed such bans.
qs: Obviously, law can drive whether humans are in the loop at all by requiring or forbidding their presence. Less obviously, law often creates incentives that encourage or discourage human inclusion.
Some were drafted before it was technologically relevant to ask whether a human should be involved in a decisionmaking process.
All too often, the law of humans in the loop sets humans up to fail.

kp.k: Regulatory arbitrage can favor either humans or automation
kp.d: The article describes incentives to retain clinicians when qualifying clinical decision support avoids FDA medical-device regulation and to retain meaningful human involvement to avoid GDPR Article 22's additional obligations. It acknowledges disagreement about nominal involvement under the GDPR and guidance rejecting token oversight. Conversely, it reports arguments and practices in surveillance and copyright enforcement where excluding humans can reduce regulatory exposure.
qs: Some laws encourage regulatory arbitrage when retaining a human in the loop allows a system’s developers or users to avoid more onerous regulation.
Thus, companies are incentivized to avoid additional regulatory obligations by putting a human in the loop.
To the extent having human involvement might implicate additional regulatory burdens, regulated entities will automate decisionmaking processes.

kp.k: Liability may reward nominal oversight or algorithmic deference
kp.d: The authors argue that allocating liability to immediate operators can encourage developers to retain powerless human scapegoats. They distinguish legitimate responsibility, supported by authority and capacity, from liability absorption that shields remote decisionmakers. Separately, they report Froomkin, Kerr, and Pineau's conditional prediction that superior medical AI could become the standard of care, constraining physician departures and contributing to skill atrophy; they emphasize that this was not the current medical standard.
qs: Notably, this incentive structure carries no requirement that the human be effective.
These humans in the loop may have little to no meaningful ability to affect the outcome, so long as they have enough nominal control to justify holding them legally liable and morally blameworthy.
They are concerned that once these systems reach a high enough level of performance, their use—and physician deference to their recommendations—will become the standard of care.
The use of AI is far from the current standard of care, and current liability rules are less friendly to algorithmic deference.

kp.k: Human participation can shield decisions from procedural challenge
kp.d: The authors report that successful US challenges to government algorithms have largely concerned procedure, including due process. They discuss teacher-evaluation litigation involving opaque algorithmic scores and argue that incorporating human participation can make procedural challenges harder. They also report a critique that GDPR Article 22's focus on final significant decisions can miss upstream automation, while noting that those systems may remain governed by the GDPR more broadly.
qs: Successful legal challenges to U.S. government use of algorithms have largely been procedural in nature.
Incorporating a human in the loop can make such procedural challenges more difficult.
Accordingly, there is a strong incentive to have a human play a role in any U.S. governmental decision that may implicate due process rights.

kp.k: Complementary capabilities do not guarantee superior combined performance
kp.d: The authors call simplistic allocation by what humans and machines do best the MABA-MABA trap, tracing it to the 1951 Fitts list. Human contextual judgment and algorithmic speed or consistency can complement one another, but interactions can also amplify weaknesses. Citing existing research rather than presenting a new experiment, they identify rubber-stamping, automation bias, skill fade, biased departures from advice, and the difficulty of supervising systems designed to exceed human performance.
qs: But merely inserting a human in the loop does not necessarily result in the best of both human and machine.
Instead, adding or maintaining a human in the loop of an automated system creates a new entity: a hybrid system.
When a human is placed in the loop carelessly, there is a high likelihood that the human will be disempowered, ineffective, or even create or compound system errors.

kp.k: Historical accidents demonstrate interaction and organizational failures
kp.d: The authors use Three Mile Island, Boeing 737 Max crashes, and the USS John McCain collision as cross-domain evidence against attributing hybrid failures solely to operators. Their accounts emphasize misleading or inadequate interfaces, deficient training, design defects, and organizational choices. The article reports that the two 737 Max crashes in 2018 and 2019 killed 346 people and that the August 21, 2017 McCain collision killed ten sailors and injured forty-eight others.
qs: The accident caused a paradigm shift in the industry’s understanding of the risks of human-machine systems, which recognized that the problem wasn’t (solely) the human or (solely) the machine.
It was the interactions between the two, exacerbated by poor interface design, interface failures, and a lack of planning or training for this particular kind of emergency.

kp.k: Human roles extend beyond checking algorithmic accuracy
kp.d: The article identifies nine nonexclusive roles: corrective, resilience, justificatory, dignitary, accountability, stand-in, friction, job-preserving warm body, and interface. Corrective roles cover factual errors, situational tailoring, and bias. Other roles concern legitimacy, participation, responsibility, slowing automation, employment, or communicating with users. The authors stress that these purposes can conflict and that preserving a human is not always intended to improve accuracy or efficiency.
qs: None of these roles are mutually exclusive; to the contrary, humans in the loop often fill multiple roles simultaneously.
And, importantly, not all of these roles are intended to make a hybrid system more accurate or efficient.
A regulator may wish to ensure that there is a human in the loop without regard to (or even with the intention of undermining) performance in the interest of prioritizing other values.

kp.k: Error correction can improve outcomes without ensuring adequacy
kp.d: As a cautionary example, the authors describe Michigan's MIDAS unemployment-fraud system, which initiated allegations and collection processes without human involvement. They report a later audit's ninety-three percent error rate and a forty-four percent error rate when a human reviewer was involved. These are reported administrative findings, not an experimental estimate of human review's causal effect. Following litigation, the state committed to human participation in every fraud determination.
qs: Unfortunately, the system was prone to error; a later audit found a ninety-three percent error rate.
In contrast, when there was a human reviewer, a mere (!) forty-four percent of alleged frauds were found to be erroneous.

kp.k: Legal legitimacy may justify humans independently of accuracy
kp.d: The authors discuss reasons for retaining humans in sentencing and other consequential decisions even if algorithms become more accurate. These include explanation, contestation, individualized context, and dignity, although they do not collectively endorse every dignitary argument. They report a study finding reduced perceived legitimacy with increased AI participation in legal decisions, while noting that data provenance was more influential than the decisionmaker's nature. Human explanations may nonetheless be post hoc rationalizations rather than faithful accounts of algorithmic reasoning.
qs: Justification may also provide some transparency about how decisions are reached or allow for subsequent contestation.
A 2021 empirical study found that as AI involvement in a legal decision increased, the perceived legitimacy of that decision decreased.
Some humans in the loop may play an only deceptively justificatory role.

kp.k: Professional augmentation arguments may conceal job protection
kp.d: The article identifies employment preservation as a distinct motive for human involvement, explicitly mentioning lawyers alongside physicians and pilots. It reports Pasquale's argument that AI should complement professionals to preserve meaningful work and economic participation, rather than adopting that position unconditionally. The authors warn that job protection can be presented as error correction and can privilege incumbents over patients, clients, other stakeholders, and system performance.
qs: Lawyers (and legal academics!) similarly emphasize the importance of keeping human lawyers involved in legal processes rather than relying fully on AI.
Warm body roles, for instance, are often cloaked in corrective arguments.
On a broader scale, protectionism is likely to entrench the interests of those already empowered and involved in system design at the expense of nonincumbents and other stakeholders.

kp.k: Role clarity must determine authority, resources, and evaluation
kp.d: The authors recommend explicitly identifying human purposes before designing oversight requirements or evaluating success. Error correction requires power to change outcomes, while genuine justification requires insight but not necessarily override authority. They recommend considering existing law, harm types, urgency, expertise, social power, and organizational setting, rather than assuming all human reviewers have equivalent capabilities.
qs: If the human in the loop is to serve an error correction role, they must be able to change the system’s result.
If they are to serve a genuine justificatory role, insight into the machine’s decision is necessary—but not the ability to change it.
Knowing what the human is meant to do is key to enabling their success.

kp.k: Safety regulation supplies adaptable models for hybrid governance
kp.d: The authors compare railroad regulation, nuclear-reactor licensing and guidance, and medical-device human-factors requirements. These provide differing levels of detail for interfaces, training, testing, documentation, and organizational risk management. They caution that the examples concern heavily regulated safety-critical systems, are not all automated, and do not establish that equally costly regulation is warranted in every setting.
qs: All three of our examples come from safety-critical systems, where expert government agencies regulate heavily because failures often result in physical injury or death.
Such heavy and costly regulation may be arguably less warranted when consequences are not life-threatening.
What is abundantly clear, however, is that merely declaring “there must be a human” will not set systems up for success or avoid failure.

kp.k: Training must calibrate trust and address organizational constraints
kp.d: The authors recommend usable interfaces, sufficient handoff time, safe failure modes, relevant expertise, and training that supports situational awareness and appropriate trust. They reject treating generalized distrust as a complete solution because overriding correct advice can also reduce performance. Organizational measures must address workload, resources, authority, contingency planning, and conflicting goals; their prescription-monitoring example illustrates how prosecution risks may undermine doctors' nominal freedom to depart from algorithmic scores.
qs: Both interface design and training can affect automation bias, a common human willingness to overinflate the likelihood that the system is correct.
But undertrust creates new problems.
Organizational design and choices regarding individual training and resourcing can make considerable differences in making the human in the loop more effective at her task.
Failures in complex systems often occur when a human gets trapped in juggling hard-to-reconcile goals (such as safety versus cost).

kp.k: The 2021 draft AI Act leaves oversight gaps
kp.d: The authors assess the 2021 proposal, not the subsequently enacted EU AI Act. They acknowledge design requirements, risk assessment, logging, monitoring, and incident reporting but criticize insufficient direct obligations on users concerning human training and working conditions. They warn that broad functional demands can overload reviewers or expose them to blame, and question self-assessment and the measurability of broad fundamental-rights goals.
qs: But by placing such an emphasis on enhancing the capacities of a human serving an “oversight” role, the Act might paradoxically end up overloading that human, or even setting up that human for blame should the system fail.
There remains, too, a question of whether the Act’s reliance on self-assessment accompanied by monitoring will be adequate to prevent capture by the regulated industries.
Hopefully, these issues will be addressed in future drafts, before the law is finalized.

kp.k: Oversight cannot alone resolve surveillance power and discrimination
kp.d: The facial-recognition case study conditionally assumes a regulator wants human involvement; it does not endorse deployment or identify oversight as the best intervention. The authors recommend clarifying corrective and other goals, considering due process and Fourth Amendment constraints, and requiring suitable procurement standards, training, independence, reporting, and testing. They stress that correcting individual identification errors does not by itself address broader policing power or systemic racism.
qs: A human in the loop would not meaningfully increase police accountability or address systemic racism.
To the contrary: it could plausibly be framed as “ethics washing” by regulators.
Should regulators believe that a human in the loop still serves a productive role, they must regulate to ensure that the human succeeds in that role.

kp.k: Other governance tools may outperform individual human review
kp.d: The authors recommend considering complements and alternatives where making oversight effective is too costly or interventionist. Options include advance risk assessments and design requirements, subsequent audits and performance metrics, explanations for using automation, participation by affected stakeholders, allocating the costs of harmful technologies to industry actors, and individual contestation rights. Their conclusion is conditional and contextual, not a universal preference for human review or autonomous decisions.
qs: The goals regulators want to serve by placing a human in the loop may sometimes be better served through other regulatory mechanisms.
Meanwhile, dignitary goals are furthered by establishing individual rights to contest certain automated decisions.
But humans aren’t a regulatory or design patch to be haphazardly inserted as a solution to problems that are really about the way the system as a whole is structured.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Crootof, Kaminski, and Price argue that integrating algorithms into decisionmaking creates hybrid systems with distinctive risks; retaining a human does not automatically improve outcomes. Existing law already shapes whether humans participate and can encourage ineffective oversight, liability shifting, or automation.
pts.d: This is primarily a cross-domain analysis of algorithmic governance, not a forecast of legal-market growth or lawyer displacement. The authors identify the 'MABA-MABA trap': allocating tasks according to assumed human and machine strengths without accounting for their interactions. They argue that automation changes human work, can undermine vigilance and skills, and can introduce interface and handoff failures. Law can require human involvement, encourage it through regulatory exemptions or liability allocation, or discourage it through efficiency incentives and performance-based duties. Including humans can also make procedural challenges to government decisions harder. For legal work specifically, they identify lawyers' adjustment of e-discovery search parameters as human participation in algorithmic decisionmaking and note professional support for retaining lawyers in legal processes. They distinguish job preservation from improvements in system performance. Their recommendation is to clarify human roles and regulate technological design, training, organizational authority, and the system as a whole, rather than treating human presence as sufficient protection.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The authors support their claims through legal analysis, cited empirical studies, accident investigations, administrative examples, and human factors engineering literature; they do not present an original legal-AI benchmark or legal-sector productivity study.
pts.d: Evidence for ineffective oversight includes cited research on automation bias, skill fade, biased responses to algorithmic advice, and limited effects of warnings about algorithmic limitations. The Michigan MIDAS example reports a 93 percent error rate in automated fraud determinations versus 44 percent when a human reviewer was involved, illustrating both possible improvement and substantial residual error. Three Mile Island, Boeing 737 Max, and USS John McCain investigations illustrate interactions among technical failures, interface design, training, and organizational decisions; these are examples of complex human-machine systems, not all modern AI systems. The authors cite NHTSA reporting, through a news account, of sixteen Tesla incidents involving disengagement less than one second before impact. This supports their discussion of dangerous handoffs, but their suggestion that Tesla may have intended to shift blame remains speculation. Legal examples include clinical decision-support exclusions under the Cures Act, GDPR Article 22, procedural litigation over government algorithms, and human factors rules for railroads, nuclear reactors, and medical devices. Their critique concerns the 2021 draft EU AI Act. An empirical legitimacy study is described in the text as a 2021 study and cited to a 2022 publication. The medical-malpractice prediction that improved AI could constrain physician discretion is attributed to Froomkin, Kerr, and Pineau and presented as a possible future mechanism, not as the authors' demonstrated finding.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The article describes conditions and law as understood at publication in March 2023, with conditional, context-dependent predictions rather than a timetable for professional replacement.
pts.d: The authors explicitly decline to endorse either human or algorithmic decisionmaking universally. Human participation can improve decisions only when the human has suitable capabilities, information, time, authority, and organizational support; alternatively, participation may serve dignity, explanation, accountability, friction, or employment goals without increasing accuracy. Their narrow analytical definition includes nominal or ineffective human involvement and does not imply meaningful oversight. Pressure to remove humans is conditional on perceived advantages in speed, cost, efficiency, or precision and the absence of countervailing legal requirements. Potential medical-malpractice pressure toward AI deference depends on AI attaining sufficiently high performance and becoming the standard of care; the authors emphasize that this was not the current position. Proposed requirements for judges to use algorithms are explicitly hypothetical and not endorsed. The safety-critical regulatory examples are qualified because their costs and intensity may be inappropriate elsewhere. The authors anticipate continued governance challenges for the foreseeable future, but no single universal solution.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups include professional decisionmakers and operators, technology developers and deploying organizations, regulators, and people subject to consequential algorithmic decisions.
pts.d: Lawyers, judges, physicians, pilots, drivers, and other operators may acquire new monitoring, corrective, explanatory, or interface responsibilities. They may also experience skill deterioration or bear blame despite limited practical control. Developers and deploying organizations may benefit from regulatory exemptions or shifted liability, while system-level regulation would require them to address design, training, working conditions, and meaningful authority. Professional incumbents may retain jobs through human-involvement requirements, potentially at the expense of clients, patients, or nonincumbents if preservation is disconnected from performance. People affected include benefit recipients wrongly accused of fraud, teachers evaluated by algorithms, defendants facing sentencing decisions, patients, and people subject to facial recognition. The authors stress that human review alone does not resolve structural concerns about surveillance, racial inequality, or police accountability. No distinct forecast is offered for law-firm size segments, legal pricing, associate leverage, ALSPs, or legal-service market shares.
